title: A Voice for the Planet
passage: Christiana Figueres was born in 1956 in a small country in Central America known as Costa Rica. It is famous for its green forests and animals. As a child, Christiana loved nature and liked to walk near rivers and trees. In 1962, she started school and finished it in 1974. Her father was once the president of the country, and her mother worked to help people.

When she grew up, Christiana studied at Swarthmore College in the USA and graduated in 1979. She joined the London School of Economics in the UK and completed her Master's degree in 1981. After that, she worked in many countries on projects to support clean development. She first worked on a project called Renewable Energy in the Americas (REIA). After that, she joined another project, Centre for Sustainable Development in the Americas (CSDA).
Later, she contributed to the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) project.

In the 1990s, she realized that burning coal and oil was changing the climate. Countries with less money suffered from many problems such as droughts and floods but rising temperatures affected them the most. Christiana understood that the world needed to use more renewable energy like solar and wind. In 2010, Christiana accepted a very difficult job and became the leader of the UNFCCC. Before that, a big meeting in Copenhagen could not end up with a result to create a strong plan to reduce pollution. Some said it was impossible for almost 200 countries to agree on anything. Christiana travelled around the world, listened to scientists, and met leaders. She asked countries to donate money for renewable energy projects instead of fossil fuels.

In 2015, Christiana led the talks that created the Paris Agreement since 195 out of 198 countries agreed to fight climate change and increase the use of renewable energy. The agreement set goals to keep global warming at safe levels and to give money to poor countries. Therefore, she became active in UN climate negotiations in 2020.

Because of Christiana's work, she received many awards and prizes. For instance, she was awarded Hero for the Planet in 2001, Legion of Honour in France in 2016 and Dan David Prize in 2019. Christiana still writes, speaks, and helps companies and governments to adopt stronger policies against climate change. Her future focus is on expanding renewable energy projects and supporting climate education for young people.

passage: Last summer, I joined a youth program that changed the way I see the world. It was called the UNICEF Children’s Climate Change Conference, held in Copenhagen, Denmark, in August 2023. Students and young leaders from more than 40 countries came together to talk about the climate problems and to share ideas on how we could protect our planet. 45 speakers shared their experiences and projects during the conference, and more than 42 workshops were organized over the week.

The previous conference in 2020 was about clean technology like electric buses, solar-powered schools, and recycling projects. However, topics such as water shortage, food security, and the effects of extreme weather on local communities were not discussed, so our group decided to explore these new issues in more detail this year.

On the first day, I joined a group discussion with students from Spain, Germany, and the Philippines. We each explained how climate change affects our countries. My friends from Spain spoke about droughts that make it hard for farmers to grow crops, while the student from the Philippines talked about stronger wind called typhoons that destroy villages. I shared how rising temperatures and pollution are problems in my country.

During the week, we worked on a project called “Youth Solutions for a Greener Future.” My team studied how renewable energy could help reduce carbon emissions. We created a small action plan for schools: installing solar panels, reducing single-use plastics, and starting tree-planting activities. On the final day, we presented our plan to environmental specialists in the Grand Hall. Later, we showed our posters and ideas in the Green Ideas Room, where students asked questions and joined our activities.

One of my favourite parts of the program was the “Global Night of Cultures,” held in Event Room. Every group shared food, music, or traditions from their country. I tried food that I had never eaten before, enjoyed African songs, and learned simple phrases in Chinese language. Some groups also showed traditional clothes and played games from their countries, but I didn’t join those activities because there wasn’t enough time.

At the end of the conference, I felt happy and excited. I understood that being a global citizen is not just about knowing other countries. It is about caring for people everywhere, protecting the environment, and working together to make the world better.

passage: Ali had always been fascinated by technology, but recently his curiosity shifted toward Artificial Intelligence (AI) and its role in language learning. He had read about AI being used in health and marketing, yet what truly amazed him was how much AI could transform English learning. As a university student eager to improve his skills, he decided to explore different AI tools that might make studying more engaging.

His journey began with AI-powered language learning apps. Unlike traditional classroom lessons where all students received the same materials, these apps offered personalised practice. Popular platforms such as Duolingo and Babbel adjusted lessons according to a learner’s strengths and weaknesses. Ali noticed that if someone struggled with grammar, the apps automatically provided more exercises in that area until confidence grew. It was almost like having a private teacher available at any time.

Next, Ali discovered the usefulness of chatbots. Applications such as Replika gave students the chance to practice English conversations without fear of mistakes. Chatbots could respond on many topics, helping users strengthen both speaking and writing skills. Ali felt that this was particularly helpful for shy learners who might hesitate to talk in real classrooms. The more conversations he practiced, the more comfortable he became.

Listening practice was another area where AI surprised him. He found that AI tools could generate audio stories or read articles aloud using natural voices. This feature exposed learners to a variety of accents and speaking speeds. Although not every accent was included, the available range was enough to sharpen comprehension skills and make learning more dynamic. Ali believed that listening to different voices built stronger confidence in understanding real-life English conversations.

Writing skills were not left behind either. Ali tried AI writing assistants such as QuillBot, which acted as a writing assistant that could rephrase and polish sentences. He also used the Grammarly App to check spelling and grammar errors and even paraphrase sentences. Together, these apps improved his writing fluency and reduced mistakes. With every essay he wrote, he felt more confident in expressing himself clearly and accurately.

Ali’s enthusiasm for these discoveries grew so much that he planned to share them with others. He decided to prepare a classroom presentation about the role of AI in English learning. He hoped that by explaining his experiences, he could inspire his classmates to explore these tools as well. For him, AI was not just a technological trend but an amazing resource on the journey of mastering English.

passage: Salim had always been fascinated by history, especially the stories of ancient civilisations. While exploring different cultures around great rivers such as the Nile, Indus, Amazon, and Ganges, he became especially interested in ancient Mesopotamia, often considered one of the birthplaces of human civilisation. This society emerged around 3500 BC in what is today Iraq, between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, and it made remarkable achievements that continue to influence the modern world.

One of the most important aspects of Mesopotamian life was agriculture. The fertile soil created by river waters supported the growth of many crops, including olives, rice, corn, and grapes. However, the main crops cultivated were wheat and barley. The increase of food led to population growth and the development of large cities such as Ur and Babylon, along with smaller urban centres like Eridu and Susa. These cities allowed people to pursue jobs other than farming, which encouraged a more diverse economy and laid the foundation of organised urban life.

Another significant achievement of Mesopotamia was its early writing system. Long before the alphabet and Egyptian hieroglyphics, Mesopotamians developed cuneiform, one of the earliest known systems of writing. They used it to record trade transactions, legal codes, and religious texts. Interestingly, personal stories were rarely written down. For writing, people experimented with tools like feathers and sticks, but the stylus proved most effective for creating wedge-shaped marks on clay tablets.

In terms of governance, Mesopotamia was divided into city-states. Each was ruled by a governor who collected taxes from the population to fund public works such as canals, temples, and defensive walls. One of the best examples of Mesopotamian law was the Code of Hammurabi, a detailed set of rules and punishments designed to bring justice and fairness in society.

Religion also played a central role in Mesopotamian life. They built amazing structures called ziggurats, pyramid-like temples that stood at the heart of their cities. These served not only as places of worship but also as symbols of political and spiritual power. The construction of ziggurats reflected both the engineering skill and deep faith of the civilisation.

For Salim, learning about Mesopotamia was more than studying the past. He realised that its achievements in agriculture, writing, governance, and religion paved the way for much of modern human society. The story of Mesopotamia demonstrated how creativity, organisation, and belief could shape cultures for thousands of years.

passage: Amal was thrilled to work on a new school project with her classmates. Their teacher had asked them to research a famous ancient structure, and Amal’s group chose the Pyramids of Giza, one of the most amazing ancient structures in the world. She couldn’t wait to share the details of their findings.

The Pyramids of Giza are located in Egypt, a country in Africa, and they are regarded as one of humanity’s greatest ancient structures. These pyramids were originally built as tombs for pharaohs, the rulers of ancient Egypt. Construction began around 2500 BC, which means they are more than 4,500 years old. The idea that such massive monuments have stood for millennia continues to astonish scientists and historians.

There are three main pyramids at Giza: the Great Pyramid of Khufu, the Pyramid of Khafre, and the Pyramid of Menkaure. Of these, the Great Pyramid of Khufu is the largest and held the record as the tallest artificial structure in the world for more than 3,800 years. This fact highlights the incredible skill and determination of the ancient Egyptians.

The pyramids were made of limestone blocks, carefully cut and moved without modern machinery. Even more impressive is the precision with which they were aligned to the four basic directions: north, south, east, and west. This accuracy shows the Egyptians’ advanced understanding of mathematics and astronomy.

Inside the pyramids, there are big rooms and passageways designed to hold the pharaohs and their belongings. Ancient Egyptians believed strongly in the afterlife, so they buried their rulers with treasures, food, and tools they thought would be useful for eternity. The pyramids became not only tombs but also symbols of faith, power, and legacy.

Over the centuries, the Pyramids of Giza have survived wars, natural disasters, and the passage of time. They remain a wonder for archaeologists, engineers, and tourists alike. In fact, they are officially recognised as one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, making them a global symbol of human creativity.

As part of their project, Amal’s group planned to create models of the pyramids, helping them to better understand their design and history. Amal was particularly eager to share this with her friend Sally, who had a passion for historical architecture. Amal thought Sally would be fascinated by how the pyramids reflect both human innovation and spiritual belief. She even dreamed that one day they could visit Egypt together and witness the pyramids’ magnificence in person.

passage: Salim had always been interested in social media platforms, and recently he decided to research the story of Snapchat, one of the most popular apps in the world. He knew his friend Bader also enjoyed using it, so he thought it would be exciting to share how the app began and how it developed into a global phenomenon.

Snapchat was created in 2011 by three friends, Evan Spiegel, Bobby Murphy, and Reggie Brown, while they were students at Stanford University. Their unique idea was to design an app where photos and messages disappeared after a short time, making communication more private. At first, the app was called Picaboo, but it was later renamed Snapchat. The new name came from combining the words “snap” and “chat”, which perfectly described the style of fast and casual communication.

By 2012, Snapchat had already become popular among young people. At that time, users were sending thousands of snaps every day, and the app was processing about 25 images per second. Just one year later, in 2013, the number rose dramatically to 4,500 images per second, showing how quickly it was expanding.

One of Snapchat’s biggest innovations was the introduction of the Stories feature, which allowed users to share a sequence of photos and videos that disappeared after 24 hours. Later in 2015, Snapchat launched Discover, a feature that gave users access to content from publishers and allowed them to add fun filters, lenses, and even change their voices. In 2017, the ‘Snap Map’ was introduced to enable users to see the locations and activities of their friends.

Salim was also amazed by some surprising facts about Snapchat. The app now has more than 347 million daily active users, and most of them are between 18 and 24 years old. Around 61% of its users are females, and about 63% of them open the app daily. In addition, more than four billion snaps are shared across the world every day. Snapchat’s daily views of videos have increased by 400% since its early years, proving its global impact.

Even with this huge success, Salim was surprised to learn that Snapchat is not the number one social media platform. Instead, it comes in the ninth place worldwide. The app in first place turned out to be Facebook, which also happens to be Bader’s favourite platform. Salim decided that his next search would be about Facebook so he could share even more interesting facts.

passage: Hassan had been away in Africa since mid-December to attend the IAOM EXPO, which began on the 13th of December and continued into the new year. To his surprise, while at the event he met his old friend, who had just arrived from Dubai. The friend invited him to visit Stone Town, the capital of Zanzibar, known as the largest and wealthiest city in East Africa. Excited, Hassan immediately agreed, curious to explore the region’s culture and history.

Stone Town was full of wonders. Hassan’s favourite site was the House of Wonders, a palace built in 1883 by Sultan Barghash bin Said, the second Sultan of Zanzibar. It was one of six palaces built under his reign. The name “House of Wonders” reflected its uniqueness, as it was the first building in East Africa to be equipped with electricity and an elevator. Hassan noticed that the main door was really wide. His friend explained that Sultan Barghash had made it extra wide so that he could enter the palace on the back of an elephant. The grand doors were beautifully decorated with phrases from the Quran, and inside, silver decorations and marble floors had been imported from Europe.

The palace served as a government building for many decades until 1990, when it was turned into a museum. Today, it displays a fascinating mix of Portuguese, English, Omani, and Swahili influences that together tell the story of Zanzibar’s unique cultural heritage. Hassan felt that the building truly represented the spirit of civilisation in the region.

After this amazing tour, Hassan and his friend felt hungry, so they went to the traditional market. They ordered the two most popular dishes which were the spice cake and Zanzibar pizza. Hassan really loved their pizza, but the cake wasn't tasty because it was very spicy for him. Later, they went to the spice farm. His mom was really interested in spices and fruits. So, He bought some spices as a gift for her.

Although he was enjoying his adventure, Hassan knew he had to return to the EXPO, which would continue until the 16th of January 2023. He planned to fly back to Muscat by plane after the event ended, carrying with him wonderful memories of Zanzibar’s history, food, and vibrant culture. The experience left a lasting impression of a land full of tradition and innovation.

passage: Sami had always been fascinated by ancient civilisations, so when he had the chance to join a tour in Southern Mexico, he eagerly accepted. He travelled with a group of Facebook friends from different continents including Europe, Africa, and Asia. Mexico, located in Central America, was once home to the mighty Mayan civilisation, one of the most famous in history.

The group spent their first five days hiking in Calakmul city, a site rich with archaeological treasures. There, Sami was amazed to see ancient texts inscribed on pottery, stone carvings, and other artefacts recovered from Mayan tombs and monuments. These discoveries gave insight into the writing system of the Maya, which Sami believed Ahmed, being an archaeology lover, would find especially fascinating.

Calakmul was also impressive because it contained about 6,750 ancient structures, including the tallest Mayan temple. Sami and his friends, being adventure lovers, took on the challenge of climbing the 45-metre-high temple. The view from the top was breathtaking, and Sami thought it was worth the effort.

Another highlight of the trip was visiting Chichen Itza, recognised as one of the Seven Wonders of the World. Its enormous staircase led to the famous Mayan calendar, which had 18 months of 20 days each, plus a sacred five-day month called Waip. Sami’s Irish friend Jonathan struggled to climb the steep staircase and missed seeing the calendar, which left him quite frustrated.

Later, Sami’s group prepared to travel to El Mirador, one of the largest cities built by the Maya. He was excited to see its advanced water-collection system and the remarkable stone bridges that reflected the Maya’s engineering skills.

Sadly, the group had only five days left to finish their tour. Sami knew there were still many sites they would not be able to explore. He advised Ahmed that when he decided to travel to Mexico, he should plan to stay for enough days to complete his project. Sami also promised to share the contact details of their helpful tour guide to make Ahmed’s trip easier. The group was scheduled to leave Mexico on the 16th of January 2023, and Sami would return home with unforgettable memories of the Mayan civilisation’s achievements.

passage: Edward was eager to write an article for his school magazine about an extraordinary environmental project called the Plastiki. He explained that he first learned about it during an online meeting with the person in charge of the project. The Plastiki may look like many other boats sailing in Sydney Harbour, but it has a unique story behind it.

The boat is eighteen metres long, six metres wide, and weighs around twelve thousand kilograms. It can carry a crew of six people and travel at an average speed of five knots. But what makes it truly remarkable is that it is built from 12,500 plastic bottles. This unusual design immediately draws attention to the problem of plastic pollution.

The idea for the Plastiki came from David Rothschild, an environmentalist who was shocked by reports on ocean pollution. He learned that humans throw away four out of every five plastic bottles they use, and that cause about 80% of sea pollution. Determined to raise awareness, he decided to construct a boat made from plastic bottles.

Recycled plastic was used in its construction, making it an eco-friendly vessel. It relies on wind and solar power as renewable energy sources. At the back of the boat, the crew maintains a small garden where vegetables are grown for meals. There’s also a special exercise bicycle that provides electricity for the boat’s computers. Even the shower is sustainable, using saltwater taken directly from the sea.

Rothschild and his team then set out on an ambitious voyage. The Plastiki sailed across the Pacific Ocean from San Francisco to Sydney, covering a distance of 15,372 nautical kilometres. During the trip, the boat passed through the ‘Great Garbage Patch’. It was a huge area in the Pacific with 3.5 billion kilogrammes of rubbish. The journey lasted 129 days, and the crew faced serious challenges, including storms, giant waves, and winds reaching speeds of over one hundred kilometres per hour.

Despite the hardships, the Plastiki succeeded in its mission. It was more than just a boat—it was a powerful message about sustainability, innovation, and the urgent need to tackle plastic pollution. Edward hoped that his article would inspire his classmates to think about the environment and to realise that creative solutions can make a difference in the fight against global waste.
